text: Time to run the loop for real. This lesson gathers a baseline from Chapter one, reads the actual execution plan of dbo dot usp_CustomerOrderHistory from Chapter two, and checks real wait statistics from Chapter five -- in that order -- until the bottleneck is a specific, named thing, not a feeling.

Query Store already has weeks of history, so there's no need to guess at normal. Querying sys dot query_store_runtime_stats for this procedure shows two very different populations of executions. For a typical consumer account, it averages about fifteen milliseconds and six hundred forty logical reads. But running it directly for a wholesale CustomerID like TrailWorks Co-op's forty-eight thousand two-thirteen, with SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON, tells a different story: about twenty-eight seconds of elapsed time and roughly a hundred eighteen thousand logical reads for one execution. That's the baseline -- this exact procedure, for this exact class of customer, costs a hundred ninety times more than normal.

The actual execution plan for the slow case looks completely reasonable at a glance: an Index Seek on IX_Orders_CustomerID, feeding a Nested Loops join into a Key Lookup against the clustered index, to fetch OrderDate, OrderStatus, OrderTotal, and ShipDate -- the columns the narrow CustomerID-only index doesn't carry. Hovering the Key Lookup operator shows it running eighteen thousand four hundred times for this one execution -- once per row the seek finds -- and its cost share of the plan is over ninety percent. For a forty-order consumer account, forty Key Lookups are invisible. For an eighteen-thousand-four-hundred-order wholesale account, that's exactly what turns a millisecond query into a twenty-eight-second one.

Chapter five's methodology says don't stop at the plan -- confirm it against what the engine was actually waiting on. Checking sys dot dm_os_wait_stats, alongside Query Store's own wait-stats breakdown during the ten AM to two PM window, shows one category dominating: PAGEIOLATCH_SH -- waits for shared latches on data pages being read from disk into the buffer pool. That's consistent with thousands of Key Lookups per execution scattered across a fourteen-million-row table, multiplied by several reps pulling wholesale histories in the same peak window.

IX_Orders_CustomerID is a non-covering index for this query. It seeks efficiently on CustomerID, but every other column the query needs triggers a Key Lookup -- cheap per row, catastrophic multiplied by eighteen thousand four hundred. This isn't the database is slow. It's a named, specific bottleneck: a missing covering index, scaling linearly with a customer's order count.
